name: David Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am David Young, 43, a senior loader operator at a large mine. I check the road and machine, move ore, then brief the next crew about a sound or vibration they should watch; I do not rush a safety check to save a few minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what gets tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like teaching newer operators and finishing a shift without a preventable fault. My partner Erin and I have two school-age children and a mortgage; our savings cover a few months, so we are careful but not at the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the report helper is worth trying if it gives operators more time around the machine. A person still needs to look at the loader before signing the sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is operating equipment, and the card says pay carries on much as it would have. I still keep an eye on staffing, because a mine can reorganize even when the technology is modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my inspection walk and compare the tool's schedule with the board for a few weeks. I would leave our savings alone and talk with my partner Erin before changing anything at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly settled about my shifts, with a small question about how management uses saved time. Erin and I have a few months saved, so one changed week would not force a big decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your partner adjust first if a shift disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone replacing the living-room sofa before touching the mortgage or the children's school costs. I'd check the actual payslip first instead of guessing about a short shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether the new tool helped the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at whether it catches the same maintenance warnings the crew finds. If it misses a fault, I would ask for a human sign-off before it is used on every shift.

say: The report helper is worth trying if it gives us more time around the **machine**.
A person still needs to look at the loader before signing the **sheet**.
think: Most of my work is **operating equipment**, and the card leaves pay much as it is.
I watch for management changes to **staffing**, even when the tool is modest.
do: Keep my **inspection walk** and compare the tool schedule with the board.
Leave our **savings** alone while we test it.
feel: I feel **settled** about my shifts, with a small question about how saved time is used.
S0.quote: A person still needs to look at the loader before signing the sheet.
fieldNote: David anchors the conversation in **equipment checks**, not AI speculation.
His moderate savings make a short shift change manageable, but he watches **staffing** decisions.
He tests the tool against a real **maintenance board** before trusting its schedule.

steps.text: Keep the loader inspection walk on every shift
Compare the tool schedule with the board for several weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the software will handle more plans and checks, while the loader work changes more slowly. We should know how the targets were set before being judged against them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do shift handovers and maintenance planning as well as operating the loader, so some senior hours could go. My hands-on work is still most of the job, and there are a few other mines within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the new report screen after a trainer shows how it checks faults. I would ask the mine's safety committee to review any faster shift target and take a short maintenance course if the mine pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about losing lead hours. Our savings could cover a short cut, not a lasting one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you want involved in setting the new targets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the lead operators and the union steward into the target discussion. We know which checks are slow because they matter and which ones are just waiting on a form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before relying on a new screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a month of running the tool alongside the existing board before relying on it. The crew should be able to report errors without being blamed for the software.

say: The software will take more **plans and checks**, while loader work changes more slowly.
Show us how the new **targets** were set.
think: Some senior hours could go because I split time between **handovers** and equipment.
There are a few other mines within reach, but less planning may still trim **pay**.
do: Try the **report screen** after a trainer shows its fault checks.
Ask the safety committee to review targets and take a paid **maintenance course**.
feel: I am **anxious** about losing lead hours. Our savings could cover a short cut, not a lasting one.
S1.quote: The crew should be able to report errors without being blamed for the software.
fieldNote: His job is mainly physical, but **handover planning** could shrink early.
David is willing to learn once the report tool has been **tested**.
He wants an **error process** that protects workers from blame for software faults.

steps.text: Practice the fault-check report screen with a trainer
Ask the mine safety committee to review faster targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people the schedules and reports change by 2028, but robots for the loader arrive around 2031. The mine should explain what work stays and who can transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shift planning can be automated quickly, and I do not know whether the same crew keeps all its hours. The three-year gap gives the physical role time, but this is close enough that Erin and I would need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the mine's written training list now and talk with our union representative about transfer rules. In 2029, I would take a paid maintenance course if it qualifies me for an open role, while keeping my operator shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, not helpless; we have a few months saved and some mines nearby, but I cannot count on a matching post. I would want a real course place before spending household money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your partner to look over with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd review the course dates, mortgage payments and children's school calendar with Erin. We would keep the emergency fund intact until the mine confirmed that training was paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during 2029 if thinking AI arrived in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no place opened in 2029, I'd stay on the loader and ask to shadow the maintenance crew during a scheduled inspection. I would keep looking for a posted internal role rather than resigning first.

say: Schedules change by **2028**, but loader robots arrive around 2031.
Explain which jobs stay and who can **transfer**.
think: My shift planning could be automated quickly, though loader work lasts **longer**.
I cannot count on finding a matching **post** nearby.
do: Ask now for the mine's written **training list** and transfer rules.
Take a paid course in 2029 if it qualifies me for an **open role**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but have some time and a few nearby mines to check.
S2.quote: I would want a real course place before spending household money.
fieldNote: He treats the 2028 date as a threat to **planning hours**, not instant robot replacement.
A paid course and confirmed **vacancy** are conditions for using household funds.
Nearby mines give some options, but he will not resign before securing a **post**.

steps.text: Ask the union about the mine transfer rules
Take a paid maintenance course for an open role
Keep operating until the course and post are confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives operators time to train before AGI in 2031, and loader robots come roughly three years later. I would ask the mine to publish the actual course places early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning part of my lead role may go first, while the machine work continues for a while. By 2034, robots could handle that work too, so I would not treat inspection as a permanent refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the mine's paid maintenance course over the next few years and ask for a technician shadow shift. In 2032, I would apply for an inspection post if a real vacancy existed, while keeping my loader shifts until an offer was written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to prepare, though I still worry about the endpoint. My experience might help with inspections, but it cannot make those jobs safe from robots forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What course would be worth taking before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the maintenance course if it includes real equipment and a certificate the other mines accept. I would check that with the training lead before signing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during 2032, the first year after AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I'd ask the supervisor whether the inspection post had a named budget and a person leaving it. If not, I would stay in operations and apply at nearby mines too.

say: Five years gives operators time to train before **2031**.
As lead, I would ask for a **worker-backed transition plan**.
think: Planning may go first, while loader work continues for a **while**.
Robots could also take inspection work by 2034, so no path is **permanent**.
do: Take the mine-paid **maintenance course** and request a technician shadow shift.
Apply in 2032 for an inspection post if a **vacancy** exists.
feel: I have room to prepare, but remain **worried** about the endpoint.
S3.quote: My experience might help with inspections, but it cannot make those jobs safe from robots forever.
fieldNote: David sees the roughly three-year gap as time to build **transferable skills**.
He questions whether inspection work survives the later **robot arrival**.
A named **vacancy** and recognized course make the move concrete.

steps.text: Apply for a posted inspection vacancy in 2032
Keep operating until an offer is in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade gives us time to prepare if the mine shares dates instead of waiting for a crisis. Thinking work changes in 2036, with robots reaching the loader around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when the robots follow, so I still need a wage. I could qualify for inspections, but I expect those jobs to change too if robots get good enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the paid maintenance course while keeping my loader shifts and save part of each overtime cheque. In 2037, I would apply for an inspection post only if the mine still had a funded position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warning feels more manageable, but it does not settle the question of income after 2039. Our savings can bridge a short gap, not years without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to know about work by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2037, our children will be young adults, and Erin and I would help them compare trade training that works across several industries. I would not steer them toward the mine just because I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during 2037, the first year after AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine for its staffing plan before deciding whether to move closer to another site. Some similar jobs are nearby, so I would compare offers before uprooting the family.

say: A decade gives us time to prepare if the mine shares **dates** early.
Thinking work changes in 2036, with loader robots around **2039**.
think: At 53 and 56, I still need a steady **wage**.
Inspection work may change too if robots become good enough, so no job is **guaranteed**.
do: Start the paid **maintenance course** while keeping loader shifts.
Save part of each overtime cheque and apply in 2037 for a **funded post**.
feel: The warning is more manageable, but income after **2039** remains unsettled.
S4.quote: Our savings can bridge a short gap, not years without wages.
fieldNote: The decade lets him qualify while keeping **current earnings**.
He expects his children to be young adults by **2037** and supports broader training.
He would compare **local offers** before moving the family.

steps.text: Complete the maintenance course while operating the loader
Save part of each overtime cheque
Apply for a funded inspection post in 2037
Help the children compare cross-industry trade courses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year version worries me most because the mine may change planning and shifts before I can prepare. Paid training, a clear transfer process and dates for any staffing change would help me and my family plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want the mine to say which courses lead to real jobs, and let crews question the plan before it is final. I can learn a proven tool, but I do not want workers blamed for choices made by software.

headlineQuote: I can learn a proven tool, but I do not want workers blamed for choices made by software.
portrait: David is a 43-year-old senior mine operator with a **technical diploma**.
He is careful with new technology and learns after it is **proven**.
His partner and two children share a mortgage and a **moderate savings cushion**.
He values worker voice and will pursue training only when it leads to a **real job**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries him because planning and shift decisions change before the household can prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training, clear **transfer rules** and early staffing dates would help David plan.
